title: Panini's Grammar Machine
description: A grammar of nearly 4,000 rules from about the 4th century BCE, how it works, and the tradition behind it

concepts.title: Nearly Four Thousand Rules
concepts.contentHtml:
In December 2022 the University of Cambridge publicized the doctoral thesis of Rishi Rajpopat under headlines about solving a "2,500-year-old" Sanskrit puzzle. The puzzle concerned one rule in the Aṣṭādhyāyī, "eight chapters," a grammar by Panini that people still study, recite and argue over.

Almost nothing is known of Panini himself. An 8th-century copper-plate inscription calls him a man of Salatura, in ancient Gandhara, in what is now northwest Pakistan, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang heard in the 7th century of a town on the Indus said to be his birthplace. His date is inferred from his language and from words such as coin names. Many scholars, including Oskar von Hinüber and Harry Falk, favor the 4th century BCE; others argue for the 5th or 6th. A story in the Panchatantra has him killed by a lion, but that one is legend.

In the usual count the grammar has 3,959 rules, called sūtras ("threads"), set out in eight chapters of four quarters each. They're so compressed that a trained reciter can get through the whole text in about two hours, and so terse that you'd find them nearly unreadable without commentary. Panini covered two varieties. One was the language of the Vedic hymns, which he labels chandas; the other was the educated speech of his own day, which he calls simply bhāṣā, "speech." The name saṃskṛta, "put together, refined," became the usual name for the language later, set against prākṛta, "natural, ordinary," for the vernaculars.

Panini was refining a tradition, not starting one. He names about ten earlier grammarians whose works are mostly lost, and his rules lean on separate lists, including a catalog of roughly 2,000 verb roots, the Dhātupāṭha.

concepts.title: How the Machine Runs
concepts.contentHtml:
Fourteen short lines list the sounds of Sanskrit, and the whole grammar is keyed to them. Together they're the Shiva Sutras, named after a legend that Shiva drummed them out. Each line is closed by a marker consonant that serves as a label. Take any sound and any later marker and you have a code for everything between. So ac (from a in line 1 to the marker c closing line 4) means "all vowels," and hal means "all consonants." About 42 of these codes, called pratyāhāras, appear in the grammar. The very first rule, vṛddhir ādaic, uses one to define the term vṛddhi as the vowels ā, ai and au.

With such codes a rule can be a few syllables long. Rule 6.1.77, iko yaṇ aci, says that i, u, ṛ and ḷ become y, v, r and l before a vowel, which is why dadhi "curd" plus atra "here" is pronounced dadhyatra. Leonard Bloomfield, in Language (1933), called the grammar "one of the greatest monuments of human intelligence." In 1967 Peter Ingerman proposed renaming the standard notation for programming-language syntax "Panini-Backus Form"; the Indologist Dominik Wujastyk later noted that the comparison ignores how Panini's rules are ordered and block one another.

When two rules could both apply, metarule 1.4.2, vipratiṣedhe paraṃ kāryam, decides between them. It's traditionally read as "in a conflict, the rule later in the text prevails," and commentators added further principles to make that work. Rajpopat argued that para means the rule applying to the right-hand part of the word being built, which lets the grammar run with very few exceptions. Specialists took the idea seriously; some thought the "2,500-year-old puzzle" framing oversold it, and its general acceptance is still being tested.

concepts.title: Grammar as Guardian of the Veda
concepts.contentHtml:
Panini stood near the end of centuries of work driven by one aim: keeping the Vedic hymns exact. The hymns were sacred sound, and a mispronounced syllable could spoil a ritual. Priestly schools memorized them in several formats at once, including the continuous text, a word-by-word version called the padapāṭha, and elaborate patterns in which words are recited in pairs, forward and backward, so that any slip would show. UNESCO proclaimed the tradition of Vedic chanting a Masterpiece of the Oral and Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2003.1 The method worked, and the Rigveda, usually dated to the second half of the 2nd millennium BCE, was handed down orally for many centuries before anyone wrote it.

Out of this came phonetics. Treatises called prātiśākhyas, each attached to a Vedic school, described how every sound is made and how sounds change at word boundaries. Indian scripts still arrange their letters by that analysis. Devanagari runs from the back of the mouth to the lips, starting with ka kha ga gha ṅa (velars), then palatals, retroflexes and dentals, and finally pa pha ba bha ma (labials). Each row runs voiceless, voiceless aspirated, voiced, voiced aspirated, nasal. The Latin alphabet has no such logic to its order.

After Panini, the tradition kept arguing. Yaska's Nirukta, a treatise on the etymology of obscure Vedic words, is usually dated before Panini. Katyayana, perhaps in the 3rd century BCE, wrote critical notes on Panini's rules, the vārttikas, and Patanjali's Mahābhāṣya, the "Great Commentary" of about the 2nd century BCE, debated both. Indian tradition calls Panini, Katyayana and Patanjali the three sages of grammar. Around the 5th century CE Bhartrhari turned grammar into a philosophy of language. Historians often describe grammar as the model science of classical India, the discipline others tried to imitate.

title: Before and After William Jones
description: The 1786 lecture, the Jesuits and merchants who noticed first, and how Sanskrit lost its crown

concepts.title: A Judge in Calcutta
concepts.contentHtml:
On 2 February 1786 Sir William Jones gave the third anniversary discourse of the Asiatic Society in Calcutta, a lecture about the Hindus. One sentence from it became the most quoted passage in the history of linguistics: "The Sanscrit language, whatever be its antiquity, is of a wonderful structure; more perfect than the Greek, more copious than the Latin, and more exquisitely refined than either, yet bearing to both of them a stronger affinity, both in the roots of verbs and in the forms of grammar, than could possibly have been produced by accident; so strong indeed, that no philologer could examine them all three, without believing them to have sprung from some common source, which, perhaps, no longer exists." He added that Gothic, Celtic and Old Persian probably belonged with them.

Jones (1746 to 1794), a lawyer already famous as a linguist, reached Calcutta in September 1783 as a judge of the Supreme Court at Fort William and founded the Asiatic Society in January 1784. He took up Sanskrit for a practical reason: courts in Bengal applied Hindu law on pandits' advice, and when pandits disagreed Jones wanted to read the texts himself. His teacher was a pandit named Ramalochana.

The passage got two things right: it pointed to grammar, not just similar words, and it allowed that the common ancestor might be lost rather than being Sanskrit itself. Elsewhere in his discourses he wrongly linked Egyptian, Chinese and Japanese to the family and left out Slavic and the Hindustani spoken around him. He also worked inside a biblical frame, writing that either the first eleven chapters of Genesis were true "or the whole fabrick of our national religion is false."

concepts.title: The Forerunners
concepts.contentHtml:
Jones was not the first European to notice. In 1583 the English Jesuit Thomas Stephens, who had reached Goa in 1579 and later wrote a long Christian poem, the Kristapurana, in a mix of Marathi and Konkani, remarked in a letter to his brother on resemblances between Indian languages and Greek and Latin. In 1585 the Florentine merchant Filippo Sassetti, writing from India to Bernardo Davanzati, listed Sanskrit and Italian pairs: deva and dio "god," sarpa and serpe "snake," and the numbers sapta, aṣṭa, nava beside sette, otto, nove. Neither letter was published until long after it could have mattered.

The idea of a lost parent language was older still. In 1647 the Dutch scholar Marcus Zuerius van Boxhorn proposed that Dutch, Greek, Latin, Persian and German descended from a vanished "Scythian" tongue, and he warned that loanwords can fake a relationship. He knew no Sanskrit. Closest of all came Gaston-Laurent Coeurdoux, a French Jesuit at Pondicherry, who in 1767 sent the Académie des Inscriptions in Paris a memoir comparing Sanskrit with Greek and Latin and noting links to German and Russian. He weighed explanations from trade and conquest to common origin. The memoir was printed only in 1808.

Why does Jones get the credit? He spoke with authority, in English, to a society whose journal, Asiatick Researches, printed the lecture in 1788 and was read across Europe. The timing helped. Charles Wilkins, who had learned Sanskrit before Jones, had just published the first English translation of the Bhagavad Gita (1785), and European readers were primed for Indian learning. Many historians of linguistics now argue that the 1786 passage changed where scholars looked more than how they worked.

concepts.title: How Sanskrit Lost Its Crown
concepts.contentHtml:
The 19th century took up Jones's hint, and at first Sanskrit looked like the parent. Friedrich Schlegel's On the Language and Wisdom of the Indians (1808) treated it as the oldest member of the family. Franz Bopp's 1816 study compared the verb systems of Sanskrit, Greek, Latin, Persian and Germanic and is usually counted as the founding work of comparative grammar; Rasmus Rask and Jacob Grimm worked out the Germanic side. Sanskrit's appeal was obvious: eight noun cases, a dual number, a rich verb system, and a native grammatical tradition that had already analyzed words into roots and suffixes.

Then came the vowels. Where Greek and Latin have e, o and a, Sanskrit usually has only a: Sanskrit ásti, Greek estí, Latin est, "is." Early scholars assumed Sanskrit kept the original vowel and the others split it. In the late 1870s several scholars, working independently, saw the law of palatals. Sanskrit ca "and" matches Latin -que and Greek te, and its palatal c is the sound Sanskrit developed from k only before a front vowel such as e. So the ancestor of Sanskrit once had e in that word and later merged it into a. Greek, not Sanskrit, kept the older vowels.

In 1879 Ferdinand de Saussure, then 21, argued from patterns inside the known languages that the parent language had sounds no descendant then known preserved. After Bedřich Hrozný identified Hittite as Indo-European in 1915, Jerzy Kuryłowicz showed in 1927 that Hittite ḫ appears roughly where Saussure's lost sounds should have been. Sanskrit still gives evidence, especially for consonants and grammar, as an elder sister of Greek and Latin.

title: Cousins in Four Languages
description: Cognate sets, Grimm's law seen from India, and the rule that links Buddha to an auction bid

concepts.title: A Family Table
concepts.contentHtml:
Line up a few everyday words in Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and Old English and the family shows itself.

  • mother: mātṛ, mḗtēr (Doric mā́tēr), māter, mōdor
  • father: pitṛ, patḗr, pater, fæder
  • brother: bhrātṛ, phrā́tēr, frāter, brōþor
  • two: dvā, dúo, duo, twā
  • name: nāman, ónoma, nōmen, nama
  • mouse: mūṣ, mûs, mūs, mūs

These are cognates: words inherited from one ancestor, not borrowed. The proof is regularity, not resemblance. Sanskrit, Greek and Latin p matches English f in word after word: pitṛ and father, Sanskrit pād- and foot. Meanings drift while sounds correspond. Greek phrā́tēr meant a member of a clan brotherhood, a phratry; the everyday Greek word for a brother was adelphós. Ganesha's mount, the mūṣaka, is a mouse or rat named from the same root as mouse.

The gods are in the table too. The Vedic sky god Dyauṣ Pitā, "Sky Father," matches Greek Zeus patēr and Latin Iuppiter, also called Diespiter. English kept a relative in Tuesday, the day of Tiw, a god whose name comes from the same root as Sanskrit deva and Latin deus.

concepts.title: Grimm's Law, Seen from India
concepts.contentHtml:
Sanskrit is the best witness for Grimm's law because it kept the old consonant contrasts nearly intact. Proto-Germanic shifted three whole series of stops; Sanskrit mostly did not:

  • voiceless p, t, k became f, th, h: pitṛ and father, tráyas and three, kás "who" and Old English hwā
  • voiced d, g became t, k: daśa and ten, dant- and tooth, jānu and knee, jñā- and know
  • aspirated bh, dh, gh became plain b, d, g: bhrātṛ and brother, bharati "carries" and bear, dadhāti "puts" and do, haṃsa "goose, swan" and goose

Sanskrit j and h in some of these are Indo-Iranian developments of older g and gh, and the silent k of knee and know was once pronounced. Even hundred fits: Sanskrit śatám, Latin centum and Greek hekatón share one ancestor. Latin kept the old k, Sanskrit turned it into ś, and Germanic, by Grimm's law, into h. This split gave the old labels "centum" and "satem" languages, though most scholars no longer treat it as the family's first division.

Grimm's law seemed to have exceptions. Sanskrit budh- "be awake, aware," the root of buddha, "awakened," starts with b, so English should have p. Instead it matches Old English bēodan "to offer," the source of bid in the auction sense. In the 1860s Hermann Grassmann, a mathematician who also translated the Rigveda, explained it. In Sanskrit and Greek, when two neighboring syllables each held an aspirate, the first lost its aspiration. The root was *bʰewdʰ-: Sanskrit and Greek lost the first aspiration, while Germanic inherited bh and regularly made it b.

concepts.title: Sister, Not Mother
concepts.contentHtml:
Online, Sanskrit is often called the mother of all languages, or at least of English. The comparative evidence says otherwise. Sanskrit, Greek, Latin and English all descend from Proto-Indo-European, and none descends from another. English door and Sanskrit dvār look like a loan but are cognates, inherited separately; mind and mantra share a root. Real cognates are often less alike than chance lookalikes. Two and dvā differ, but by rule. English bad and Persian bad "bad" sound the same and mean the same, and linguists cite them as a textbook coincidence.

Particular myths circulate widely. A much-forwarded list of "facts about India" says navigation comes from a Sanskrit word navgatih. It comes from Latin navigare, from navis "ship" and agere "drive." Latin navis is cognate with Sanskrit nau "boat," so the claim turns a real kinship into a false borrowing. Another story says NASA declared Sanskrit the best language for computers. It grew from a 1985 article in AI Magazine by Rick Briggs, who compared the Indian grammarians' unambiguous sentence analysis with knowledge representation in artificial intelligence. The article was no NASA policy, and no space agency programs in Sanskrit.

The most elaborate versions came from P. N. Oak (1917 to 2007), who claimed that Vatican came from Sanskrit vatika "hermitage" and Christianity from "Krishna-niti." The scholar Srinivas Aravamudan treats these as delusional etymologies. The test for any claim is the same: regular sound correspondences across many words, dated records, and a plausible route of contact. Sanskrit is a close cousin of English through Proto-Indo-European, and a donor of loanwords that traveled by caravan, ship and empire.

title: From Sanskrit to Marathi
description: Old, Middle and New Indo-Aryan, the sound changes that wore words down, and Marathi's own history

concepts.title: Old, Middle, New
concepts.contentHtml:
Among the oldest Indo-Aryan words written down in their own time are numbers in a horse-training manual. Around 1400 BCE Kikkuli, a Hurrian horse master from the kingdom of Mitanni in northern Syria, set out a chariot-horse program that survives in Hittite copies. Its technical terms include aika-, tera-, panza-, satta- and nāwa-wartanna, "one, three, five, seven, nine turns," close to Sanskrit eka, tri, pañca, sapta, nava. The Rigveda is older in composition but survived by memory, not on tablets.

Linguists divide Indo-Aryan history into three stages. Old Indo-Aryan is Vedic and Classical Sanskrit. Middle Indo-Aryan covers Pali, the Prakrits and, late, Apabhramsha, "fallen away." The edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE, among the earliest deciphered Indian inscriptions, are in Prakrits, not Sanskrit. New Indo-Aryan, including Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati and Marathi, appears in writing late in the 1st millennium CE.

The tree is not as simple as "Sanskrit begat Marathi." Classical Sanskrit was a learned standard held steady by Panini's rules. The Prakrits grew from spoken Old Indo-Aryan dialects that were close to it but not identical, which is why most linguists treat Sanskrit as the best-recorded relative of their ancestor rather than the ancestor itself. Sanskrit and Prakrit also lived side by side for centuries. In Sanskrit drama kings and Brahmins speak Sanskrit while most women and servants speak Prakrit; Kalidasa's heroine Shakuntala speaks Prakrit. Many sung verses are in Maharashtri, the Prakrit of the Deccan, which the 7th-century critic Dandin ranked above all others. Maharashtri is the ancestor of Marathi and Konkani.

concepts.title: Hand, Seven, Work: How Words Wore Down
concepts.contentHtml:
Two sound changes explain much of the distance from Sanskrit to Marathi and Hindi. In Middle Indo-Aryan, consonant clusters assimilated into double consonants. In New Indo-Aryan the double consonant was simplified and the vowel before it grew long, keeping the syllable's weight.

  • hand: hasta to Prakrit hattha to Marathi hāt, Hindi hāth
  • seven: sapta to satta to sāt
  • work: karman to kamma to kām
  • ear: karṇa to kaṇṇa to kān
  • fire: agni to aggi to āg

Prakrit grammarians named the two kinds of words that result. A tadbhava, "arising from that," is an inherited word that went through such changes. A tatsama, "same as that," was taken back from Sanskrit later, unchanged, for religion, learning and government. So Marathi has doublets much like English royal and regal: hāt and hasta "hand," kām "work" and karma "deed," kān and karṇa "ear," nāv and nām "name." The inherited word is usually the everyday one.

Inherited Marathi words still carry Indo-European cousins. Bhāū "brother" comes from bhrātṛ, a cognate of brother. Dāt "tooth" matches Latin dent- and English tooth. Āg goes back to agni, cognate with Latin ignis, the source of ignite. And nāv also means "boat," from Sanskrit nau, a cognate of Latin navis and Greek naus, behind navy and nautical.

concepts.title: Marathi's Own Story
concepts.contentHtml:
Marathi is probably first attested in a copper plate of 739 CE from Satara. A short line at the foot of the colossal Bahubali statue at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, from about 981 CE, is often cited as an early specimen, though some classify it as late Prakrit, and the earliest stone inscriptions wholly in Marathi date from about 1012 CE. After 1187 the Yadava kings of Devagiri used Marathi more and more in their inscriptions, and the poet-saint Dnyaneshwar's commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, the Dnyaneshwari, traditionally dated 1290, became a central work of Marathi literature.

Marathi grew up beside the Dravidian languages Kannada and Telugu, and under the Deccan sultanates it absorbed Persian vocabulary that is still everyday: bāg "garden," kārkhānā "workshop," shahar "city," jamin "land." Shivaji pushed back. A glossary of state usage that he commissioned, the Rājavyavahārakośa, completed in 1677, offered Sanskrit replacements for Persian and Arabic terms of government. One count of administrative documents finds the Persian share of vocabulary falling from about 80 percent in 1630 to 37 percent by 1677. Choosing a tatsama could be a political act.

One Marathi word lives in English. Mongoose, recorded from the 1690s, came through Portuguese from Marathi muṅgūs, itself ultimately from a Dravidian word. Its spelling was reshaped to look like goose, a folk etymology, which is why the plural is mongooses. Marathi had about 83 million first-language speakers in the 2011 census, and in October 2024 the Government of India recognized it as a classical language. It is written in Devanagari; the cursive Modi script once used for administration is now met mostly in old documents.

title: Sugar, Spice and Chess
description: Words that left India by caravan and ship centuries before the British arrived

concepts.title: Sugar Took Three Roads
concepts.contentHtml:
English holds one Sanskrit word three times without knowing it. Sanskrit śarkarā meant "gravel, grit," and then the granular sugar that Indian cooks made from cane juice. Accounts of Alexander's campaign, preserved by later Greek writers, mention an Indian reed that yields honey without bees. The word itself went west by three separate routes:

  • through Persia and Islam: Middle Persian šakar, Arabic sukkar, Old Italian zucchero, Old French çucre, Middle English sugre, sugar
  • through Greek: Pali sakkharā, Greek sákkharon, Latin saccharum, English saccharine and the sweetener saccharin
  • by sea: Malayalam cakkara or Tamil cakkarai, Portuguese jágara, English jaggery, the unrefined cane or palm sugar of South Asia

Spanish azúcar kept the Arabic article, as-sukkar, "the sugar." Candy came separately. Sanskrit khaṇḍa means "piece, fragment" and also lumps of sugar; Persian qand and Arabic qandī gave Old French sucre candi and Middle English sugre candy, crystallized sugar. Some etymologists prefer a Dravidian source for the Persian word, comparing Tamil kaṇṭu "hard candy," so the Sanskrit origin is likely but not settled.

The name of the subcontinent made a similar journey. Sanskrit Sindhu, the Indus river, became Old Persian Hindu, with the regular Iranian change of s to h, and Greek Indos, which dropped the h. India and Hindu descend from it, and so does indigo, from Greek indikon, "the Indian dye."

concepts.title: Spices with Southern Roots
concepts.contentHtml:
Many words that reached Europe through Sanskrit are Dravidian at the root; the pepper coast was the Tamil and Malayalam south. Pepper runs back through Old English pipor, Latin piper and Greek péperi to an Indian source like Sanskrit pippalī, which named long pepper, a cousin of black pepper. Sanskrit probably took the word from a Dravidian language; compare Tamil tippali.

Ginger came through Latin zingiberi and Greek zingíberis from a Prakrit form like siṃgivera, beside Sanskrit śṛṅgavera. The Sanskrit is often explained as śṛṅga "horn" plus vera "body," for the knobbly root, but that is probably folk etymology; the word looks like Tamil and Malayalam iñci-vēr, with vēr "root." Orange began as Sanskrit nāraṅga "orange tree," itself from a Dravidian word, then Persian nārang and Arabic nāranj. Italian once said narancia; in Italian and French the n dropped off, probably because speakers heard it as part of the article, so that French une norenge became une orenge. English took the fruit's name from Old French in the 14th century and used it for the color from about 1510.

Some southern words skipped Sanskrit entirely. Curry is Tamil kaṟi, a spiced sauce or relish eaten with rice, taken up by Portuguese and then English traders; Hannah Glasse's The Art of Cookery (1747) printed a recipe "To make a Currey the India way." Indian cooks name dishes individually, and the catch-all category is largely a European creation. Catamaran is Tamil kaṭṭumaram, from kaṭṭu "tie" and maram "tree, wood": a raft of logs lashed together. English later gave the name to twin-hulled boats.

concepts.title: Chess Words: Indian Board, Persian Pieces
concepts.contentHtml:
Chess began in India as caturaṅga, "having four limbs," an epic word for an army of elephants, chariots, cavalry and infantry. The game is clearly attested by the 6th to 7th century CE; Bana's Harshacharita, of about 625 CE, contains what is usually cited as the earliest mention of the game by that name. A Middle Persian text tells how an Indian king sent the game to the court of Khosrow I, who reigned from 531 to 579, and Persian čatrang kept the Sanskrit name. Arabic, which has no ch or hard g sound, reshaped it as šaṭranj, and Persian later borrowed that form back. Spanish ajedrez and Portuguese xadrez, from Andalusian Arabic, still carry caturaṅga inside them.

The English chess words, though, are Persian, not Sanskrit. Chess is Old French esches, plural of eschec "check," from Persian shāh "king," the warning call when the king is attacked. Checkmate is Persian shāh māt. Māt is usually glossed "stunned, helpless, at a loss"; the popular gloss "the king is dead" reads it as Arabic māta "he died," a competing view. The exchequer, England's royal treasury, is named for the checkered cloth on which officials counted money, laid out like a chessboard. Rook is Persian rukh, the piece that descends from the chariot.

Other pieces kept older identities in other languages. The bishop was once the elephant: Arabic al-fīl, from Persian pīl, survives as Spanish alfil. The queen began as the firzān or fers, a counselor that moved one square diagonally, and became the modern queen only in late 15th-century Europe. Players still move an Indian army under names that passed through Persian, Arabic and Old French.

title: Raj Words and Spiritual Words
description: Hobson-Jobson's glossary, words that carried colonial fears, and how karma, guru and avatar changed in English

concepts.title: Hobson-Jobson
concepts.contentHtml:
In 1886 Henry Yule and Arthur Coke Burnell published Hobson-Jobson, a glossary of "Anglo-Indian colloquial words and phrases" with more than 2,000 entries. Burnell had died in 1882, and Yule completed most of the work; William Crooke edited a second edition in 1903. "Hobson-Jobson" was British soldiers' version of the Shia mourning cry "Yā Ḥasan! Yā Ḥosain!" heard at Muharram, and Anglo-Indians used it for festive occasions in general. Linguists still speak of the "law of Hobson-Jobson" when borrowers reshape a foreign word to fit their own sounds, as Spanish cucaracha became cockroach.

Many entries were words of a British household in India. Jungle is Hindi jaṅgal, from Sanskrit jāṅgala "arid, sparse country." English recorded it from about 1776, in Nathaniel Halhed's translation of a Hindu law code, and English pushed the sense toward dense tropical forest. Cot is Hindi khāṭ, from Sanskrit khaṭvā "bedstead," probably Dravidian in origin. Pyjamas is Hindustani pājāma, from Persian pā "leg" and jāma "garment": loose trousers that Europeans adopted as nightwear. Persian pā is a distant cognate of English foot.

Bungalow is Hindi baṅglā or Gujarati baṅglo, "of Bengal": a house in the Bengal style, typically on one story with a veranda. The first houses in England called bungalows went up at Westgate-on-Sea in Kent around 1869 to 1870 as seaside holiday homes. Shampoo is Hindi cā̃po, the command form of cā̃pnā "to press, knead," recorded in English in 1762 for a massage. Sake Dean Mahomed, from Patna and the first Indian to publish a book in English, ran "shampooing" vapor baths in Brighton and was appointed shampooing surgeon to George IV. Only around 1860 did shampoo come to mean washing the hair.

concepts.title: Loot, Thug, Juggernaut
concepts.contentHtml:
Some Raj words carried colonial fears. Loot is Hindi lūṭ "booty, plunder," from Sanskrit, either loptra "stolen property" or the root luṇṭ "rob." It appears in English from 1788, in the era of Company conquest; American slang later used it for money or any haul.

Thug is Hindi ṭhag "swindler, cheat." Many dictionaries trace it to Sanskrit sthaga "cunning," from a root meaning "to cover, conceal"; others call the Prakrit source of uncertain origin. British officials applied it to gangs who joined travelers, then strangled and robbed them. William Henry Sleeman's campaign of the 1830s, run largely through informers called approvers, produced about 1,368 convictions from 1826 to 1835 and 4,224 by 1847. Officials described an ancient, hereditary fraternity of ritual killers devoted to Kali. Historians such as Kim Wagner accept that the gangs were real but see them as bandits, and find the Kali references came mostly from Sleeman's own comments and leading questions; Martine van Woerkens gives more weight to religion. Philip Meadows Taylor's novel Confessions of a Thug (1839) made the word a sensation, and by then it could mean any ruffian.

Juggernaut is Jagannātha "lord of the world," a form of Vishnu worshipped at Puri in Odisha. At the annual Ratha Yatra crowds haul his image through the streets on huge wooden chariots. The Franciscan friar Odoric of Pordenone, who traveled in India in the 1320s, described devotees throwing themselves beneath an idol's chariot, and later British writers, many of them missionaries, repeated such scenes. Deaths did happen, some in crowd crushes and some apparently deliberate, but scholars think European accounts inflated their number. By the mid-19th century a juggernaut was any crushing, unstoppable force; in Britain it is also a heavy truck.

concepts.title: Karma, Guru, Avatar
concepts.contentHtml:
The last layer is religious vocabulary, borrowed by scholars first. Karma, Sanskrit karman "act, action," first appears in English in 1785, in Charles Wilkins's translation of the Bhagavad Gita. In Hindu, Buddhist and Jain thought it is the force of a person's actions shaping future lives; everyday English has shrunk it to payback within one life. Yoga, "yoking, union," comes from the root of English yoke. For most Westerners it means postures, though the classical Yoga Sutras (by a Patanjali most scholars distinguish from the grammarian) center on meditation.

Guru first meant "heavy," then "weighty, venerable," and so a teacher; it shares an Indo-European root with Latin gravis, the source of grave and gravity. English used it for a spiritual teacher from the 17th century and, in the 20th, for any influential adviser. The popular explanation gu "darkness" plus ru "remover" comes from a late Upanishad and is a traditional folk etymology. Pundit, Sanskrit paṇḍita "learned man," named Brahmin scholars, including those who advised British courts; English later stretched it to any expert, and now to media commentators.

Avatar, Sanskrit avatāra "descent," from ava "down" and tṛ "cross," names a god's descent to earth in bodily form, as with Vishnu's avatars Rama and Krishna. William Jones first used it in English, in a poem of about 1784. In the mid-1980s Lucasfilm's online game Habitat used it for a player's on-screen figure, and Neal Stephenson's novel Snow Crash (1992) spread that sense. The direction reversed: a god descends into a body, while a gamer projects a figure into a virtual world. Mantra, from the root of mind, went from Vedic verse (English from 1808) to meditation phrase to office slogan.
